blocks.body:
Pick an integer $n$ at random from $1,\dots,x$. Being divisible by $2$ happens with probability about $\frac12$, by $3$ with probability about $\frac13$, and by both with probability about $\frac16$: these events behave like independent coin flips. So the number of distinct prime factors $\omega(n)=\sum_{p\mid n}1$ is, morally, a sum of independent random variables, one for each prime, and probability theory predicts how it is distributed.

Probabilistic number theory makes this precise. Its flagship result, the Erdős–Kac theorem (1940), says that $\omega(n)$ obeys the central limit theorem: it is approximately normal with mean and variance $\log\log n$. The same viewpoint explains why the average of an arithmetic function can be very different from its typical value, and it supplies the random models used to make conjectures about primes.

blocks.title: Divisibility events are nearly independent
blocks.body:
For distinct primes $p_1,\dots,p_k$, by unique factorisation $n$ is divisible by all of them exactly when $p_1\cdots p_k\mid n$, so
$$\frac1x\#\{n\le x:\ p_1\mid n,\dots,p_k\mid n\}=\frac1x\Bigl\lfloor\frac{x}{p_1\cdots p_k}\Bigr\rfloor=\frac1{p_1}\cdots\frac1{p_k}+O\Bigl(\frac1x\Bigr).$$
So the indicator functions $\mathbf 1_{p\mid n}$ behave like independent Bernoulli random variables $X_p$ with $\Pr(X_p=1)=\frac1p$, as long as the product of the primes involved is small compared with $x$. The model breaks down for large primes: no $n\le x$ is divisible by two primes greater than $\sqrt x$, although the model would allow it.

In the model, $\omega$ corresponds to $\sum_{p\le x}X_p$ ([[random-variables]]), with mean $\sum_{p\le x}\frac1p$ and variance $\sum_{p\le x}\frac1p(1-\frac1p)$. By [[mertens|Mertens' theorem]], $\sum_{p\le x}\frac1p=\log\log x+M+O(1/\log x)$ with $M\approx0.2615$, so both are $\log\log x+O(1)$. The [[limit-theorems|central limit theorem]] then predicts that $(\omega(n)-\log\log x)/\sqrt{\log\log x}$ is approximately standard normal. The proof has to deal with the failure of independence for large primes.

blocks.title: Normal order
blocks.body:
An arithmetic function $f$ has normal order $F(n)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$
$$\#\{n\le x:\ |f(n)-F(n)|>\varepsilon F(n)\}=o(x)\qquad(x\to\infty).$$
That is, for almost all $n$ (all but a set of density zero), $f(n)=(1+o(1))F(n)$. This describes the typical size of $f$, which need not match its average.

blocks.title: Hardy–Ramanujan theorem, with Turán's variance bound
blocks.body:
For $x\ge3$,
$$\sum_{n\le x}\bigl(\omega(n)-\log\log x\bigr)^2\ll x\log\log x.$$
Consequently $\omega(n)$ has normal order $\log\log n$ (Hardy and Ramanujan, 1917).

Write $L=\log\log x$ and use $\sum_{p\le x}\frac1p=L+O(1)$ and $\pi(x)=O(x/\log x)=O(x)$.

First moment. Swapping sums,
$$S_1=\sum_{n\le x}\omega(n)=\sum_{p\le x}\Bigl\lfloor\frac xp\Bigr\rfloor=x\sum_{p\le x}\frac1p+O(\pi(x))=xL+O(x).$$

Second moment. $\omega(n)^2=\sum_{p\mid n}\sum_{q\mid n}1$, counting ordered pairs of prime divisors. Pairs with $p=q$ give $\omega(n)$ again; pairs with $p\ne q$ need $pq\mid n$. So
$$S_2=\sum_{n\le x}\omega(n)^2=\sum_{\substack{p\ne q\\ pq\le x}}\Bigl\lfloor\frac x{pq}\Bigr\rfloor+S_1\le x\sum_{\substack{p,q\le x}}\frac1{pq}+S_1=x\Bigl(\sum_{p\le x}\frac1p\Bigr)^2+S_1=xL^2+O(xL).$$

Expanding the square,
$$\sum_{n\le x}(\omega(n)-L)^2=S_2-2LS_1+L^2\lfloor x\rfloor\le xL^2+O(xL)-2L\bigl(xL+O(x)\bigr)+xL^2=O(xL).$$

Normal order. By Chebyshev's inequality, for any $\varepsilon>0$ the number of $n\le x$ with $|\omega(n)-L|>\varepsilon L$ is at most $O(xL)/(\varepsilon L)^2=O\bigl(x/(\varepsilon^2L)\bigr)=o(x)$. To replace $L=\log\log x$ by $\log\log n$, note that for $\sqrt x<n\le x$ we have $\log\log x-\log2\le\log\log n\le\log\log x$, and the $n\le\sqrt x$ are only $o(x)$ of them.

blocks.title: Erdős–Kac theorem
blocks.body:
For every real $t$,
$$\frac1x\#\Bigl\{n\le x:\ \frac{\omega(n)-\log\log n}{\sqrt{\log\log n}}\le t\Bigr\}\to\Phi(t)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^te^{-s^2/2}\,ds\qquad(x\to\infty).$$
The same holds with $\omega$ replaced by $\Omega(n)$, the number of prime factors counted with multiplicity.

blocks.title: How the Erdős–Kac theorem is proved
blocks.body:
We sketch the method of moments; the details are omitted.

1. Truncate. Let $y=x^{\varepsilon(x)}$ with $\varepsilon(x)\to0$ slowly, and $\omega_y(n)=\#\{p\le y:\ p\mid n\}$. A number $n\le x$ has at most $1/\varepsilon(x)$ prime factors above $y$, so $\omega(n)-\omega_y(n)\le1/\varepsilon(x)$. If $\varepsilon(x)$ tends to $0$ slowly enough that $1/\varepsilon(x)=o(\sqrt{\log\log x})$, this difference does not affect the limit. Also $\sum_{y<p\le x}\frac1p=\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon(x)}+o(1)$ is $o(\sqrt{\log\log x})$, so the centring is unchanged.
2. Compare moments. For fixed $k$, expand $\sum_{n\le x}\bigl(\omega_y(n)-\mu_y\bigr)^k$, where $\mu_y=\sum_{p\le y}\frac1p$. It becomes a sum over $k$-tuples of primes $\le y$ of counts of $n\le x$ divisible by given products, which by the computation above equal the model probabilities up to errors $O(1)$ each. There are at most $\pi(y)^k\le y^k=x^{k\varepsilon(x)}$ tuples, so the total error is $o(x)$. Hence the $k$-th moment of $\omega_y(n)-\mu_y$ over $n\le x$ agrees asymptotically with that of $\sum_{p\le y}(X_p-\frac1p)$ for independent $X_p$.
3. Apply the CLT. The variance of the model sum tends to infinity and the summands are bounded, so the normalised model sum tends to the normal distribution, with convergence of all moments.
4. Conclude. The normal distribution is determined by its moments, so convergence of moments implies convergence in distribution for $\omega_y$, hence for $\omega$.

Kac's original heuristic and Erdős's sieve argument were combined in 1940; the moment proof above is due to later authors (Halberstam, Billingsley, and in a particularly clean form Granville and Soundararajan). Rényi and Turán showed that the rate of convergence is $O(1/\sqrt{\log\log x})$, which explains why the theorem is almost invisible in numerical data (Example 3).

blocks.title: Beyond ω: additive functions and random models
blocks.body:
A function $f$ is additive if $f(mn)=f(m)+f(n)$ whenever $\gcd(m,n)=1$. Both $\omega$ and $\log\frac{\varphi(n)}{n}=\sum_{p\mid n}\log(1-\frac1p)$ are additive, and the probabilistic model treats every additive function as a sum of nearly independent contributions $f(p^k)$ ([[arithmetic-functions]]). Two broad theorems:
- Erdős–Wintner: a real additive function has a limiting distribution if and only if the three series $\sum_{|f(p)|>1}\frac1p$, $\sum_{|f(p)|\le1}\frac{f(p)}p$ and $\sum_{|f(p)|\le1}\frac{f(p)^2}p$ all converge. For $f=\log\frac{\varphi(n)}n$ we have $f(p)\approx-\frac1p$, so all three converge, and $\frac{\varphi(n)}{n}$ has a limiting distribution (Schoenberg, 1928); its mean is $\frac6{\pi^2}$.
- When the series diverge, the distribution must be normalised; Kubilius developed a general theory of this case, in which Erdős–Kac is the model example and a central limit theorem holds under suitable conditions.

For the primes themselves, Cramér's model (each $n$ is "prime" independently with probability $1/\log n$) predicts the right density and is the source of conjectures on gaps ([[prime-patterns]]). It must be corrected for divisibility by small primes; the corrected version reproduces the Hardy–Littlewood prime tuple conjectures, including the constant in the [[twin-primes|twin prime]] asymptotic. Maier's theorem shows that even so, the model fails in very short intervals. Probabilistic heuristics are reliable guides only when the arithmetic correlations are put in by hand.

blocks.title: Example 1: the average of ω
blocks.body: Show that $\sum_{n\le x}\omega(n)=x\log\log x+Mx+O(x/\log x)$, and compare with the computed average for $x=10^6$.
blocks.solution:
As in the proof, $\sum_{n\le x}\omega(n)=\sum_{p\le x}\lfloor x/p\rfloor$. Writing $\lfloor x/p\rfloor=x/p-\{x/p\}$, the fractional parts contribute at most $\pi(x)=O(x/\log x)$, and Mertens' theorem gives $x\sum_{p\le x}\frac1p=x\log\log x+Mx+O(x/\log x)$.

For $x=10^6$: $\log\log x\approx2.626$, and the prediction for the average is $2.626+0.2615\approx2.887$. The actual average of $\omega(n)$ over $n\le10^6$ is $2.854$; the difference $0.033$ is within the $O(1/\log x)$ error, as $1/\log10^6\approx0.072$.

blocks.title: Example 2: typical versus average number of divisors
blocks.body: Show that $2^{\omega(n)}\le\tau(n)\le2^{\Omega(n)}$, and deduce that for almost all $n$, $\tau(n)=(\log n)^{\log2+o(1)}$. Compare with the average $\frac1x\sum_{n\le x}\tau(n)\sim\log x$.
blocks.solution:
If $n=\prod p_i^{e_i}$ then $\tau(n)=\prod(e_i+1)$, and $2\le e_i+1\le2^{e_i}$ for $e_i\ge1$. Multiplying over $i$ gives $2^{\omega(n)}\le\tau(n)\le2^{\Omega(n)}$.

By Hardy–Ramanujan (and the same argument for $\Omega$, whose average exceeds that of $\omega$ only by $O(1)$), for almost all $n$ both $\omega(n)$ and $\Omega(n)$ are $(1+o(1))\log\log n$. Then $\tau(n)$ is between $2^{(1+o(1))\log\log n}$ and the same with $\Omega$, i.e. $\tau(n)=(\log n)^{\log2+o(1)}$ with $\log2\approx0.693$.

So the typical $n$ has about $(\log n)^{0.69}$ divisors, but the average is $\log x$ ([[arithmetic-functions]]): a thin set of integers with very many divisors dominates the mean. At $x=10^6$ the mean of $\tau(n)$ is $13.97$ while the median is $8$; $(\log x)^{\log2}\approx6.2$.

blocks.title: Example 3: what the data look like at x = 10^6
blocks.body: Tabulate $\omega(n)$ for $n\le10^6$ and compare with the normal approximation of mean and variance $\log\log x\approx2.63$.
blocks.solution:
Counting gives: $\omega=0$ once ($n=1$), $\omega=1$ for $78734$ numbers, $2$ for $288726$, $3$ for $379720$, $4$ for $208034$, $5$ for $42492$, $6$ for $2285$ and $7$ for $8$. (No $n\le10^6$ has eight distinct prime factors, since $2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17\cdot19=9699690$.)

The mean is $2.85$, but the variance is only $0.98$, far below $2.63$. The reason is that $\omega$ is a sum of only a few effective "coins": the primes that can occur in an $n\le x$ have $\sum1/p$ about $2.9$, and the constraint that the product is at most $x$ creates strong negative correlations among large primes. As $\log\log x$ grows by $1$ only when $x$ is raised to the power $e$, the Gaussian shape emerges extremely slowly, in line with the Rényi–Turán rate $1/\sqrt{\log\log x}$. The theorem is true; it is just not something one sees on a computer.

blocks.title: Example 4: an exact identity behind 2^ω
blocks.body: Show that $2^{\omega(n)}=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)^2$, and deduce $\sum_{n\le x}2^{\omega(n)}=\sum_{d\le x}\mu(d)^2\lfloor x/d\rfloor$. Conclude that the average of $2^{\omega(n)}$ is of order $\log x$, much larger than its typical size $(\log x)^{\log2}$.
blocks.solution:
The squarefree divisors of $n$ are the products of subsets of the $\omega(n)$ distinct primes dividing $n$, so there are $2^{\omega(n)}$ of them, and $\mu(d)^2$ is the indicator that $d$ is squarefree. Summing over $n\le x$ and swapping the order: each squarefree $d\le x$ divides $\lfloor x/d\rfloor$ integers $n\le x$.

Since the squarefree numbers have density $\frac6{\pi^2}$ ([[smooth-powerful]]), partial summation gives $\sum_{d\le x}\mu(d)^2/d=\frac6{\pi^2}\log x+O(1)$, hence $\sum_{n\le x}2^{\omega(n)}=\frac6{\pi^2}x\log x+O(x)$. Numerically at $x=10^6$ the ratio $\frac{1}{x\log x}\sum_{n\le x}2^{\omega(n)}$ is $0.665$, approaching $\frac6{\pi^2}\approx0.608$ slowly because of the $O(x)$ term.

The typical value is $2^{(1+o(1))\log\log n}=(\log n)^{\log2+o(1)}$, so again the mean is dominated by a small set of $n$ with unusually many prime factors.

blocks.body:
- Typical is not average. $\tau(n)$ and $2^{\omega(n)}$ have averages of order $\log x$ but typical sizes $(\log n)^{0.69}$.
- The independence model holds only for small primes. Two primes above $\sqrt x$ cannot both divide $n\le x$, and ignoring this distorts variances (Example 3).
- Do not expect to see Erdős–Kac numerically. With $\log\log10^{100}\approx5.4$, even astronomically large $x$ give few effective coin flips.
- "Almost all" means all but a set of density zero; there are infinitely many exceptions, such as the primorials, with $\omega(n)\sim\log n/\log\log n$.
- Random models of the primes (Cramér) are heuristics. They need corrections for small primes and still fail in very short intervals (Maier).

The inputs are [[mertens|Mertens' theorems]] and the [[pnt|prime number theorem]], and the arithmetic functions studied are those of [[arithmetic-functions]]; the probability is the [[limit-theorems|law of large numbers and central limit theorem]] applied to sums of [[random-variables]]. Sieve methods ([[sieve-basics]]) are the tool for controlling the dependence between divisibility events, and the largest prime factor of a random integer, governed by Dickman's function, comes from [[smooth-powerful|smooth numbers]]. Random models of the primes generate the conjectures in [[prime-patterns]] and [[twin-primes]]. The same philosophy, that arithmetic quantities look like sums of independent random variables, appears in the distribution of values of $L$-functions and in the [[probabilistic-method|probabilistic method]] in combinatorics.

1. Show that $\sum_{n\le x}\Omega(n)-\sum_{n\le x}\omega(n)=O(x)$, so $\Omega$ also has normal order $\log\log n$.
2. Using Chebyshev's inequality and the variance bound, show that the proportion of $n\le x$ with $|\omega(n)-\log\log x|>(\log\log x)^{3/4}$ is $O((\log\log x)^{-1/2})$.
3. Show that the proportion of $n\le x$ with $\omega(n)=1$ tends to $0$, and identify its order of magnitude.
4. Show that $\frac1x\sum_{n\le x}\frac{\varphi(n)}n\to\frac6{\pi^2}$ by writing $\frac{\varphi(n)}n=\sum_{d\mid n}\frac{\mu(d)}d$.
